one_pager.big_idea: Scientists separate what they can see (observations) from what they think it means (inferences), and they change their story when new evidence appears.
goals: I can tell the difference between an observation and an inference.
I can change my inference when I get new evidence.

flow.what: Seat groups from the plan as students arrive; hand out the baseline skills check and read each stem aloud in English. Students work alone in silence; do not help with answers.

Collect skills checks; hand out the survey and read each statement aloud; students tick one face each. While the surveys are collected, show the Today slide (1 minute): goals in English, a student reads the Chinese, thumbs check.
Stage 1 snow tracks: 'Who walked here? What do scientists do?' Quick pair guesses in any language; introduce the series in one sentence.
Observation versus inference with the melted snowman picture; thumbs up or down on four statements; model 'I observe ___.' and 'I infer ___ because ___.'

Footprint puzzle in groups: Stage 1 card, Stage 2 after about 3 minutes, Stage 3 after about 6 minutes. Students write observations and inferences for each stage and change their story; keep asking 'How do you know?'
Two Reporters share stories; 'Can we be 100% sure?'; exit ticket strip; first logbook line ('What I did'). Collect exit tickets at the door and logbooks into the class box.

one_pager.practical: Footprint puzzle (paper): groups open three reveal cards one stage at a time and record observations and inferences.
one_pager.assessment: Baseline skills check (out of 20) and interest survey, both entered in the tracker as the Week 1 baseline for Week 10; exit ticket with one observation and one inference; first logbook page.
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Keep bags and coats under the tables so walkways stay clear.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'I observe ___.' 我观察到___。 'I infer ___ because ___.' 我推断___，因为___。 'At first I inferred ___. Now I infer ___ because ___.' 起初我推断___。现在我推断___，因为___。 Chinese talk welcome in the puzzle and the 'Can we be sure?' discussion; Reporters share in English with frames. Seat each Band 1 student beside a Band 3 buddy who explains in Chinese but never writes the answer; the exit ticket may be written in Chinese. Traps: 'observe' and 'observation' are both 观察; 'infer' (推断) is not 'guess' (猜); 'track' means a line of footprints.
watch_out: Protect the full 15 minutes of the skills check: do not explain science words or help, and never go through or hand back the papers (the same paper is used in Week 10).
Students treat an inference as just a guess: an inference must be linked to an observation with 'because'.
Keep the Stage 2 and 3 envelopes on the teacher desk until about 3 and 6 minutes in; if time is short, skip Stage 2.
one_pager.next_week_link: Logbooks stay in the class box and puzzle cards go back in their envelopes in stage order. Read the exit tickets before Week 2. The Week 2 Do Now is the mystery cups (moved from Week 1), reusing the observe and infer frames: this week make 12 mystery cups, print and cut the question sort cards, and find a hardback book and practise the paper-on-book drop.

one_pager.big_idea: Scientists can test an idea in their heads first (a thought experiment), then turn their curiosity into questions that an experiment can answer.
goals: I can tell the difference between a testable and a not testable question.
I can write a testable question and a prediction with a reason.

flow.what: Groups shake, listen and weigh two sealed mystery cups (do not open) and write 'I observe ___. I infer ___ because ___.' for each; then the Today slide with goals and key words (about 1 minute). Slides 1 to 2.
Class vote: a heavy ball and a light ball dropped together, which lands first? Predictions with 'because'; opening of the Galileo story. Slides 3 to 4.

Walk through the six-panel Galileo storyboard; teacher drops book and flat paper, book and crumpled paper, then paper on top of the book, with a prediction before each; introduce testable questions. Slides 5 to 8. If short, skip the paper-on-book drop.

Question sort: 12 cards into testable or not testable (8 min); then the worksheet: three testable winter questions, each with a prediction and a reason, with Core, Stretch and Challenge tiers (10 min). Slides 9 to 10. If short, two questions.
'Heavier things fall faster: always, sometimes or never?' Pair talk in any language, share in English with a frame; exit ticket; logbook line. Slides 11 to 12. Collect exit tickets and logbooks.

one_pager.practical: Groups handle sealed mystery cups and sort question cards; only the teacher does the book and paper drops.
one_pager.assessment: Question sort checked in class (note groups with three or more errors); three testable winter questions on the worksheet (Rubric strand 1, Questioning and predicting); exit ticket: identify the testable question and write a prediction with a reason.
hazards: Small objects in the mystery cups (choking): cups stay taped shut and are never opened; nothing in mouths.
Falling book: only the teacher drops it, from about 1 m, onto a table or the floor, with feet and hands clear.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'I observe ___. I infer ___ because ___.' 'I predict ___ because ___.' 'This question is testable because we can change ___ and measure ___.' 'Does ___ change ___?' Chinese talk welcome in the card sort and the always / sometimes / never talk. Band 1: sit beside the language buddy, who reads the Chinese on each card; the Do Now inference, prediction and exit ticket may be in Chinese. Traps: 'light' means not heavy (轻), not lamp light (光); 'fall' is a verb (下落), not autumn; 'testable' (可检验的) is not an exam test (考试).
watch_out: Students think heavier things always fall faster, or that paper falls slowly because it is light: use the flat and crumpled sheets (same mass, different fall) and insist on 'sometimes'.
Practise the paper-on-top drop beforehand: the sheet must be smaller than the book cover or it slides off.
Do not reveal the cup contents; the A to L key is on the kit card, so keep that card on the teacher desk, not on the tables.

one_pager.big_idea: Measurements always vary a little, so scientists repeat them, work out a mean and look carefully at any result that does not fit.
goals: I can record repeat measurements with the correct units and calculate a mean.
I can spot an anomaly and explain why I leave it out of the mean.

flow.what: Retrieval: name the IV, DV and one control in a salt-and-ice test; why did two people time one drop as 1.62 s and 1.85 s? Then the Today slide (goals and key words, about 1 minute). Slides 1 to 2; worksheet Do Now box.
Teacher drops one L spinner once from 2 m; three volunteers time the same drop and the three times go on the board. Why are they different? Slide 3.

Units in the table heading, repeats, mean = total ÷ number of values, anomaly; worked example (8 cm: 2.05, 1.12, 2.11 s gives 2.08 s without the anomaly, 1.76 s with it); students try one mean in Core C. Slides 4 to 7; worksheet Core A to C.

Say, show, check on Slide 8; groups get their spinner envelopes back and do three repeats for each wing length (9 drops, same Measurer, about 8 minutes), record, circle any anomaly with a reason and calculate the means; worksheet Stretch and Challenge; sample data card if data is poor. Slides 8 to 9. If short: two repeats, or only 4 cm and 8 cm.

'Include it or leave it out?' (6 cm: 1.70, 1.66, 2.40 s): pair talk in any language, share in English with a frame; why timings differ; exit ticket; logbook line. Slides 10 to 12. Recorders put the results table and spinners back in the envelope.

one_pager.assessment: Completed group results table with means and circled anomalies with reasons (kept in the group envelope for Week 5 graphing); exit ticket: circle the anomaly in Hana's results and calculate the mean without it (checkpoint question 6 skill); note groups whose data is unusable (they use the sample data in Week 5).
hazards: Falls: never stand on chairs or tables; the Dropper stands flat on the floor (use the 1.8 m mark if needed).
Tripping: keep bags off the floor under the drop marks.
Scissors (repairs only): carry with the points down.
Paper clips: do not unbend them or point them at anyone.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'The anomaly is ___ because ___.' 'I will leave it out of the mean because ___.' 'The times are different because ___.' 'To make it more accurate, we could ___.' Chinese talk welcome during 'Include it or leave it out?'. Band 1: sit beside a Band 3 language buddy, who reads the Chinese line of each task and explains it in Chinese but never writes the answer; Core A uses the picture icons, Core B the bilingual word bank, Core C the picture strip; in Core D record times as numbers and tick a reason; the Do Now, My thinking and exit ticket may be in Chinese with the English key words. Traps: 'mean' is the average (平均值), not 'unkind'; 'second' is a unit of time (秒), not second place; 'Repeat 1' in a heading is the test number (第1次).
watch_out: Students divide by 3 even after leaving out an anomaly: check this in every group.
Anomalies rubbed out, or any result a group dislikes called an anomaly: circle it, write a reason, leave it out of the mean, never rub it out.
Groups run out of time for the means: keep the same Measurer and aim to finish the 9 drops in about 8 minutes; if short, two repeats per wing length or the sample data card.

one_pager.big_idea: A graph turns a table of numbers into a picture, so we can spot the pattern and write a conclusion that uses the data as evidence.
goals: I can choose between a bar chart and a line graph and plot my results accurately.
I can write a conclusion using "As the ___ increases, the ___ ___."

flow.what: Quick mean and units: 1.40, 1.46, 1.52 s gives a mean of 1.46 s; wing length is in cm. Hand out the group envelopes with the Week 4 results tables. Slide 1; worksheet Do Now box.

Checkpoint alone and in silence: read each stem in English, then its Chinese gloss; Chinese accepted for every written answer; no help with answers; collect at exactly 10 minutes. Show the Today slide (goals and key words) while papers are counted, no extra time. Slides 2 to 3.
The same spinner means as a bar chart and as a line graph: 'Which tells the story better?' Vote and give a reason. Slide 4.

Word or group: bar chart; number: line graph. Independent variable on the x-axis, dependent variable on the y-axis; plot with small crosses; one line of best fit, ignoring the anomaly. Quick 'bar or line?' examples and a plotting demo. Slides 5 to 7.

Copy the means (own group's or the sample data card) into the table, label the axes, plot crosses, draw a line of best fit and write a conclusion with the frame; Core, Stretch, Challenge. Teacher checks labels, units, crosses and the line. Slides 8 to 9. If short: Core plots and does the conclusion cloze; line of best fit as a class demo.

'Bar or line?' with four cards: vote with BAR or LINE cards and justify with the frame (A bar, B line, C bar, D line); can we trust the pattern at 20 cm? Exit ticket and logbook line; collect exit tickets and worksheets; tell the class a new teacher leads from next week. Slides 10 to 12. If short, two cards.

one_pager.practical: No practical: after the checkpoint, each student plots a line graph of the Week 4 spinner means (or the sample data) and writes a conclusion.
one_pager.assessment: Checkpoint out of 12 (mark scheme in assessment/Checkpoint_Y7.md), entered in tracker column Q before the handover note; graph and conclusion on the worksheet (Rubric strand 4, Analysing and concluding); exit ticket: bar chart or line graph with a reason (answer: bar chart, because type of material is a word or group).
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Carry rulers and pencils safely; do not wave them near faces.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'As the ___ increases, the ___ ___.' 'We drew a ___ because the independent variable is a ___.' 'When the wings were ___ cm, the mean fall time was ___ s.' 'I predict ___ because ___.' Chinese talk welcome in the Hook vote and 'Bar or line?'. Band 1: sit beside the language buddy, who explains in Chinese and never writes the answer; follow the picture cues through Core A to C; Chinese answers accepted everywhere, including the checkpoint. Traps: 'plot' means mark a point (描点), not a story; axis singular, axes plural; increase and decrease (use arrow gestures); 'line graph' (折线图) is not 'line of best fit'.
watch_out: The checkpoint overruns: collect at exactly 10 minutes and count papers against the register.
The sample data card's Mean column is blank: groups using it must calculate the means first, leaving out the 1.12 s anomaly at 8 cm (1.31, 1.68, 2.08 s).
Dot-to-dot lines or swapped axes: wing length goes on the x-axis, and the line of best fit is one smooth line close to all the points, not through an anomaly.
one_pager.next_week_link: Enter checkpoint scores in tracker column Q, then complete one handover note per class and book the 30-minute walkthrough before Week 6. Keep two sets of S, M and L spinners as the demo, the logbooks and the graphs (note who struggled with axes and plotting: Week 9 depends on it). Run the strip trial for Weeks 7 to 8 this week (Plan B strips must be made now to dry) and keep 2 spare plain strips for the Week 8 Hook. Week 6 starts the ice project: ice cube rescue (Plan A) or keep it warm (Plan B), using the freezer decision from Week 4.

one_pager.big_idea: A thermal insulator slows down heat transfer, so a coat on a snowman slows the heat moving from the warm air into the snow, and it melts more slowly.
goals: I can plan and carry out a fair test to compare thermal insulators.
I can explain, using my results, why a coat slows down melting (or cooling).

flow.phase: Do Now (start the ice / dress the cups)
flow.what: Plan A: Safety Officers collect a cup of 4 bagged cubes from the cool box at the door; groups wrap three bags in three materials, leave bag A bare and put each bag in its labelled cup; the Recorder writes the start time and the teacher writes the class start time on the board. Plan B: groups wrap cups B to D (side jacket, lid square beside the cup) and leave cup A bare; the teacher fills the jug to about 50 °C. Then the Today slide: goals and key words (1 minute). Slide 1 (Plan A) or 2 (Plan B), then Slide 3.

Snowman concept cartoon: read the four speech bubbles (a student reads each Chinese gist line) without saying who is right; hands-up vote with 'I agree with ___ because ___.' Plan B: while pairs talk, the teacher pours 150 ml of warm water into every cup, then groups fit the lid squares. Slides 4 to 5; worksheet Core A.

Heat moves from warm to cold (cold does not move); a coat makes no heat but slows heat transfer both ways; today's fair test with the Week 3 gestures (I change / I measure / I keep the same; cup A is the control); safety slide. Plan B: in the first 2 minutes Measurers take start readings A, B, C, D and Recorders start the stopwatch at cup A. Worksheet Core C. Plan A Slides 7, 8, 9, 11; Plan B Slides 6, 7, 8, 10, 12.

Hands off the cups. Variables table (Core D), prediction with a reason, then Stretch and Challenge while the ice melts or the water cools; the teacher checks tables and predictions. Plan B: at 15 minutes on each group's stopwatch (about minute 25) take end readings in the same order and calculate each drop. Slide 13 (Plan B also Slide 16).

flow.phase: Think and Reflect part 1 (Plan B: Do continues)
flow.what: Plan A: hand out the Week 7 planning frame in the group folders; groups choose a project question and draft the independent variable on page 1 only (Chinese talk welcome). Plan B: finish the temperature drops, ranks, Stretch and Challenge. Slide 14 (Plan A).

flow.phase: Do part 2: measure (Plan B: planning frame)
flow.what: Plan A: 'Stop the clock': gloves on, unwrap, pour each bag's meltwater into the measuring cylinder, read at eye level and record in Core B; never cut this slot. Plan B: planning frame page 1 (choose a question and draft the independent variable). Slide 15 (Plan A) or Slide 14 (Plan B).

Two Reporters give the best and worst material with the frame; back to the cartoon: 'Who was right?' (Owen; Bo partly right); exit ticket; logbook line if time; Lead Scientists put the planning frame in the group folder. Slides 17 to 18.

one_pager.practical: Plan A: groups wrap bagged ice cubes in three materials (one bare as the control) and measure the meltwater after about 29 minutes; Plan B: groups wrap cups of teacher-poured warm water (about 50 °C) and measure the temperature drop over 15 minutes.
one_pager.assessment: Mini fair-test write-up on the worksheet (variables, prediction, results, conclusion): supporting evidence for Rubric strands 2 to 4. Planning frame page 1 drafted and kept in each group's folder for Week 7. Exit ticket: the best insulator with a number and unit from the results and a reason. The incoming teacher notes who leads in each group and who needs language support.
hazards: Plan A: cold skin from ice: gloves for handling ice for more than a minute; ice stays in sealed bags until the measuring slot.
Both plans: wet floor: cups stand on trays; mop spills straight away.
Plan B: warm water (about 50 °C, never hotter than 55 °C): only the teacher prepares and pours it; students handle wrapped cups only and do not move cups once full.
Plan B: thermometers can break: spirit or digital only, never mercury; lay them flat; tell the teacher at once; the teacher clears broken glass and counts thermometers first at clean-up.
No tasting, eating or drinking anything, including ice and water; wash hands after the practical.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'I agree with ___ because ___.' 'The best insulator was ___ because it had the least meltwater / smallest temperature drop: ___.' 'A coat slows down heat moving from ___ to ___.' 'We kept ___ the same because ___.' Chinese talk welcome during the cartoon vote and the planning frame discussion. Band 1: sit beside a language buddy, who explains each step in Chinese and never writes the answer; start with Core B (letters, times and numbers), then Core A (vote from the picture cue and the 概要 gist line); Core C on the Chinese paragraph with the bilingual word bank or the draw-a-line version; Core D by sorting the bilingual variable cards. Answers in Chinese count in every Core task. Traps: 'insulator' (隔热材料) here means heat, not electricity (绝缘体); 'a coat keeps you warm' does not mean the coat makes heat; 'drop' means the temperature goes down (下降).
watch_out: The timing only works if the ice (Plan A) or the cup jackets (Plan B) start in the Do Now: kit trays on the tables before students arrive. Plan A: never cut the 4-minute measuring slot; cut Think part 1 to 2 minutes instead.
Misconceptions: 'coats make heat' and 'cold comes in'. Heat moves, cold does not; a snowman makes no heat, so the coat only slows heat getting in. Foil is not the best just because it is shiny.

Plan B: about 3.6 litres of warm water are needed but the jug holds about 2 litres, so refill or use the second jug and check about 50 °C each time; groups start their stopwatches at different times, so watch each group's 15 minutes.
one_pager.next_week_link: Keep the planning frames (page 1 drafted) in the 6 group folders; they come back at the start of Week 7, which finishes the plan and makes the samples (thin strips about 12 cm x 2 cm x 5 mm in foil troughs) in the last 10 minutes. Dry and keep the reusable foil, fabric and bubble wrap. During this week, for Week 7: run the strip trial (Week 7 kit card) and buy untreated sawdust now; Plan A: book freezer space for the class set (two shallow trays in one drawer); Plan B: flour, salt and a drying shelf.

Core D sort cards: the Band 1 and 2 card strip ('CUT HERE') sits in the middle of worksheet page 3, so cutting it out also cuts into page 4 on the back, and no scissors are listed for students (nor for the teacher's cutting of material squares, jackets and lid slits). Plan A cups: is the cup that holds each group's 4 bagged cubes a fifth cup (30 cups per class) or one of cups A to D (24)?

Plan A ice: the kit card says freeze two trays the day before (28 cubes), while the Teacher Guide (Week 4 row) says request ice from the canteen and Sections 7 and 8 say about 24 cubes. Which source, and how many Year 7 classes have this lesson on the same day (each needs its own 28 cubes, two trays and freezer space)?

Plan A measuring: the kit card allows 25 ml or 10 ml cylinders and the Teacher Guide (Week 5 row) allows a kitchen scale. With 2 to 10 ml of meltwater expected, are 10 ml cylinders available? If a scale is used, the worksheet heading (ml) would need to read g.

one_pager.big_idea: Adding fibres to a brittle material makes a composite that is harder to break, and a good plan (question, variables, prediction, method, risks, results table) lets us test this fairly.
goals: I can plan a fair test of my own: question, variables, prediction with a reason, method and risk assessment.
I can make identical samples that change only one thing, and label them clearly.

one_pager.practical: Pairs make and label about 9 thin fibre-reinforced strips per group in identical foil troughs: ice strips for freezing (Plan A) or salt-dough strips for drying (Plan B).

hazards: [Plan A] Wood dust: untreated natural sawdust or pet-bedding shavings only, never MDF (it contains resin glues); sawdust pre-portioned and kept damp, water goes in first, never blown or tipped from a height.
[Plan A] Wet floor: mop spills straight away. Freezer: only the teacher carries the trays and puts them in the freezer.
[Plan B] Flour allergy: check the school allergy list first; allergic students take a non-dough role and do not touch the dough.
[Plan B] Never eat the dough (very salty, not food); knead inside the closed bag so no flour dust escapes; untreated sawdust only; wash hands after.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'Does the ___ change the ___ of the ___?' 'I predict ___ because the fibres ___.' 'We will keep ___ the same because ___.' 'The hazard is ___. It could ___. We will ___.' Chinese talk welcome during planning; each group writes its plan in English with key words. Band 1: sit beside the language buddy; start with Core B (tick lists, copy sample codes from the bilingual code key), then Core A with the Chinese gist lines and picture cues; owns Box 2 and Box 8 of the frame; reasons in Boxes 4 and 5 may be in Chinese. Traps: 'strength' (强度) is a property of a material, not muscles; 'mould' (模具) is the container, not the fungus (霉菌); the hazard is the thing, the risk is what could happen.
watch_out: Every group must include the control (plain ice, no fibre or 0 g) and change only one thing (fibre type at 0.6 g each, or amount of sawdust); check against the class project board before anyone makes samples.
The strip trial must be done before this lesson (Plan B in Week 5 so the strips dry); write its decision (strip size, Week 8 span) on the class project board.
Labels in pencil only and never cut labelling; trays stay flat and level (Plan B: peel the foil and turn the strips on day 3).
one_pager.next_week_link: Week 8 is test day: samples come out of the freezer (Plan A, at least 24 hours, flat and level) or off the drying shelf (Plan B, turned on day 3) at the start of the lesson, and groups run two rigs in parallel to reach three repeats. Keep the approved planning frames in the group folders and the class project board on the wall. During this week, for Week 8: books, string, plastic bags, measuring jugs, catch trays, towels, gloves and a mop.

one_pager.big_idea: A test is only as good as the way it is carried out: every sample is tested in exactly the same way, every result is recorded, and repeats show us how much results vary.
goals: I can carry out a strength (or melting) test carefully and safely, in exactly the same way for every sample.
I can record repeat results with units and notice anything unusual.

flow.what: Trays of samples (Plan A from the cool boxes, Plan B from the drying shelf) and folders go out; role cards checked. Safety Officer reads the kit card hazards aloud, Recorder copies sample codes into the results table, the others build two rigs. Today slide and goals.
Hold up a plain and a fibre sample: which will hold more water, and how will each break? Quick hands-up prediction.

Demonstrate one rig step by step without snapping a sample: 10 cm span, loop at the centre, 25 ml pours with a 5-second wait. Explain the recording rule and the parallel roles, then the safety slide. Plan A melting groups start their 15-minute test.

Two rigs per group in parallel. Test every sample in a mixed order and record every result in ml with a note on how it broke. Aim for 3 repeats (minimum 2); calculate means if time. Plan A: one strip out of the box at a time, tested within 1 minute of peeling.
Recorders copy results onto the class project board. Discuss one odd result ('Anomaly or not?') using the frame card. Exit ticket, then tidy: water back in the jug, mop, wash hands.

one_pager.practical: Groups test their Week 7 strips to breaking on two water-bag strength rigs in parallel (Plan A: up to two groups run a 15-minute melting test instead; Plan B: dough strips, strength test only).
one_pager.assessment: Raw results table with repeats and notes (main evidence for Rubric strand 3, Doing and recording); each group's results on the class project board (photographed for Week 9); exit ticket with one result and its unit, one thing that was hard to keep the same, and the goal self-check.
hazards: Hanging bag of water drops when the strip snaps: a catch tray (bucket or deep bowl) under every bag; feet and hands clear; the pourer kneels to the side, never under the bag.
Wet floor, the biggest risk today: towels on every table, mop and bucket by the door, mop spills at once and stop a group's testing until the floor is dry; water from the bags goes back into the jug.
Plan A, cold: gloves to peel foil or hold ice for more than a minute.
Plan B, dough: never eat the dough or broken pieces; students with a flour allergy pour or record only; everyone washes hands after.
one_pager.language_note: Chinese talk is welcome while testing. Results and notes are written in English with key words, but a note in Chinese also counts: mark the science and praise the English key word. Frames: 'It snapped at ___ ml.', 'The anomaly is ___ because ___.', 'It was hard to keep ___ the same because ___.' Traps: load (负载) is not loud; snap means break suddenly, not take a photo; volume (体积) is an amount of liquid, not loudness. Band 1: sit beside the language buddy with a doing job on Rig 1 (pourer or watcher), build the rig from the bilingual diagram, and answer the exit ticket in Chinese if needed.
watch_out: Water on the floor: stop that group's testing and mop before carrying on.
Every sample tested the same way: 10 cm span measured each time, loop at the centre, gentle 25 ml pours, no pressing on the strip (Plan A: strips tested within 1 minute of peeling).
Early snaps or 'bad' results left out: record every result with a note on how it broke, and push for 3 repeats (accept 2).

one_pager.big_idea: Pooling everyone's results gives stronger evidence than one group alone; the right graph shows the pattern, and a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning conclusion and an honest evaluation say what the evidence means and how sure we can be.
goals: I can choose the right graph for our data and write a conclusion with a claim, evidence (numbers) and reasoning (science).
I can explain one problem with our test, how it affected the results, and how sure we are.

flow.what: Group folders returned; students finish any Week 8 group means (leaving out anomalies) and check them against the class results table; Today slide (1 minute).
'Snow Owls 292 ml, Ice Foxes 300 ml: who is right?' Pair talk in any language: why do results differ, and do we trust one group or the whole class?

Pooling (class mean = mean of the group means); bar or line vote (word or group: bar chart; number: line graph); teacher models a CER conclusion and an evaluation sentence with the sample data; students complete Core A and B.

Poster panels by role: each student completes their worksheet section (Core C, Stretch, Challenge), writes their panel card and the group glues panels onto the A3 poster; teacher checks axes, units and CER numbers and gives out sample class data where needed. Aim to glue the first panels by minute 12.
Self-assessment slip (4 minutes); groups split the 2-minute Week 10 talk with the talk frame card; exit ticket; teacher collects worksheets, slips and posters.

one_pager.practical: No practical: groups pool the class data, choose a graph, and write, cut out and glue panel cards onto an A3 investigation poster.
one_pager.assessment: Poster: main evidence for Rubric strands 1 to 5 (collected; the teacher pencils in draft levels before Week 10). Individual worksheets show who wrote what. Self-assessment slips are compared with the teacher's judgement (a gap of two levels or more means a 1-minute conversation in Week 10). Exit ticket records each student's talk part for Week 10.
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Scissors for the panel cards: carry scissors with the points down.
one_pager.language_note: Chinese talk welcome while deciding the claim and the evaluation. Panels are written in English with key words, or (rule J, from October 2026) as a Chinese sentence with the English key words or the English frame completed with the language buddy; the student presents that panel in Week 10. Band 1: sit beside the language buddy, find sample rows by the Chinese labels on the A3 board table, copy axis labels from the bilingual bank, and tick and copy a prepared reasoning sentence; Chinese answers count for every Core task. Traps: claim 主张 is a scientific answer, pool 汇总 is not a swimming pool, mean is 平均值.
watch_out: Students treat their own group's result as the right answer, or think a line graph is always better: the class mean is better evidence, and type of fibre (a word) needs a bar chart.
Conclusions that only say what was done, and improvements like 'be more careful': check each conclusion answers the question with two numbers and science reasoning, and each improvement is specific.
Time: prepare the class results table beforehand, as pooling from scratch will not fit in 18 minutes; if short, finish Panels 1, 4 and 5 today and Panels 6 and 7 at the start of Week 10.
one_pager.next_week_link: Keep the posters flat (the teacher reads them and pencils in draft levels for strands 1 to 5 before Week 10), the talk frame cards in the group folders and the exit tickets (who presents which part). Posters go up in talk order before the Week 10 Expo; print the skills check, survey, peer feedback slips and question cards in advance.

one_pager.assessment: Final skills check (same paper as Week 1; tracker column S, growth calculated by the tracker); interest survey (columns U to Z); strand 6 judged from the talk record and strands 1 to 5 confirmed from the posters (draft levels pencilled in after Week 9), entered in columns AC to AH. Peer feedback slips can support strand 5; Expo notes and exit tickets feed the teacher comments and programme summary. Then awards, certificates and skills reports.
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Posters are on walls or display boards: keep the walkways in front of them clear of bags.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: answering 'That is a good question. Our evidence shows ___, but it does not show ___.'; asking: read the question card aloud; big question 'Scientists find things out by ___.' The talk frame card has one frame per part, and students may read from it; a student who freezes may give one sentence in Chinese and then the key words in English. Band 1: sit beside the language buddy, who reads the Chinese frame for the student's part and the Chinese line of their question card before Talk 1; the student rehearses once in Chinese and presents the results part (numbers and graph, as planned in Week 9). In the Expo notes, circle the pre-printed choices for what each group changed and measured and copy one number with its unit from the poster. Chinese answers count for every Core task; the exit ticket may be answered in Chinese by pointing to a week icon. Strand 6 is judged on the clarity of the science, not on grammar or accent.
watch_out: The skills check is never shortened (same paper and conditions as Week 1). If time is short, cut talks to 90 seconds, ask only three questions (after talks 2, 4 and 6) and move feedback slips to the gallery walk; never skip the survey.

Fix the order of talks before the lesson (each group is asked by the next; the first group asks the last) and label each feedback slip with the group the student asks, or questions and slips go astray.
Final certificates usually cannot be given today (strand 6 is judged today and Most Improved needs the marked skills check): thank the class and announce when and where they will be presented.
one_pager.next_week_link: Last lesson of the series. Keep the posters up for the gallery walk with the feedback slips on the back, then photograph them and store them flat. Mark and enter the skills checks and surveys (columns S and U to Z) before any papers are returned; keep the talk record for strand 6. Certificates and skills reports within a week. Store question cards, talk frames and the other reusable kit in the labelled Ice Engineers box for next year, and write three lines for next year's teacher.

one_pager.big_idea: Detectives and scientists separate what they can see (observations) from what they think it means (inferences), and they trust evidence more than opinion.
goals: I can sort statements into observations and inferences.
I can write an observation and an inference about the scene, and say what evidence would check the inference.

flow.what: Seat groups at fixed tables as they arrive; hand out the skills check and read the instructions once; students work alone for 15 minutes (5-minute warning); collect at once.
Collect skills checks; hand out the 6-question smiley survey; show the Today slide (goals and key words) while surveys are collected.
Case alert: read the briefing and the note over Slides 5 and 6; tell the Song Ci story in one minute; students open their case files.
Observation vs inference with the glass example; point to eye = observe, tap head = infer; class shows O or I for 3 statements.

Say, show, check on Slide 9; groups study the scene map; worksheet Core (tick O or I for 8 statements), then Stretch (3 observations with squares, 3 inferences), then Challenge (a test for one inference; evidence or opinion).
Meet the four suspects; thumbs vote on 'Chef Zhou is too nice to take it' (opinion); exit ticket with one O and one I; worksheet into the case file.

one_pager.practical: No practical: paper scene map task, with an optional look-only scene table at the front.
one_pager.assessment: Baseline Skills Check (15 minutes, out of 20) and interest survey go into the tracker Week 1 column; papers are filed and never returned before Week 10. Exit ticket shows who can separate observation from inference. Evidence log row 1 is started (or finished in the Week 2 Do Now).
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Optional scene table: look only. No touching, tasting or smelling the evidence.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'I observe ___ at square ___.' 'I infer ___ because ___.' 'This is an opinion because ___.' Pair talk in Chinese is welcome; key words are written in English. Traps: 'evidence' is uncountable; 'infer' vs 'inference'; 'suspect' as noun (嫌疑人) and verb (怀疑). Band 1: sit beside a Band 3 buddy who explains in Chinese but never writes the answer; Core uses the Chinese lines and bilingual map labels; exit ticket uses the A3 wall map and the bilingual frames; Stretch and Challenge are glossed, not required.
watch_out: Start the skills check the moment students sit down; it takes the full 15 minutes. Never go through or return the papers before Week 10.
Sensible guesses get called observations ('The powder is sugar'). Ask: 'Can you see that it is sugar, or are you guessing?'
Students who spot the mop bucket by the puddle or 'safe and cold' have found real clues: praise them, note their names, confirm nothing.
one_pager.next_week_link: Week 2 is fingerprints. Every case file must hold its suspect cards (the Week 2 Do Now uses them); case files stay in the class box, filed by group. Finish evidence log row 1 in the Week 2 Do Now if not done today. If time ran short, the Song Ci story and the suspect slide move to Week 2. Keep pens A to D, the pre-test strips and the note for Week 3.

one_pager.big_idea: Scientists sort things into groups (classify) and count how common each group is; how common a feature is decides how strong it is as evidence.
goals: I can take my own fingerprint and classify it as a loop, whorl or arch.

flow.what: Four questions answered from the suspect cards in the case file; check roles are given out; finish evidence log row 1 if not done; Today slide with goals and key words (about 1 minute). Slides 2 to 3.

one_pager.practical: Each student takes their own fingerprints with soft-pencil graphite and clear tape onto a record card (right index first), classifies them as loop, whorl or arch with a magnifying glass, and adds one tally to the class survey.
one_pager.assessment: Fingerprint record card (kept in the case file); class tally table and bar chart on the worksheet; evidence log row 2 and the suspect tracker 'Fingerprint' column; exit ticket (scene print type, who is ruled out, strong or weak and why) shows who understands common vs rare as evidence.
hazards: Graphite on fingers: wash hands after taking fingerprints; wipe tables.
No pencils or tape in mouths.
Take only your own fingerprints.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'My fingerprint is a ___ because the lines ___.' 'This sample matches ___ because ___.' 'This evidence is strong / weak because ___.' Chinese talk welcome while classifying and in the Think pair talk. Band 1: sit beside a Band 3 language buddy who reads the Chinese line of each task but never writes the answer; worksheet order Core b, a, c, d; Chinese answers count, and the exit ticket may use 箕形纹 and 被排除 from the fold-under word bank. Traps: 'loop' and 'arch' are everyday words with new meanings here; 'tally' is new for most; say 'fingerprint type' (纹型), not 'the same fingerprint'.
watch_out: 'Same type means same fingerprint' and 'a matching type proves who did it': every print is unique but there are only three main types. The Think answer is 'sometimes', and the evidence is weak because three of four suspects (and about 2 in 3 people) have loops.
Smudged prints come from pressing too hard or sliding the tape: use lots of graphite and a gentle press. Insist on one tally per student, right index finger only, so the survey is fair.
Some classes have no arches: use it ('24 people is not the whole world'). Label the board tally rows exactly as on Slide 9 so Band 1 students copy by label, not position.

one_pager.big_idea: Testing every sample in the same way, in the same order, and recording the results in a grid lets us identify an unknown by comparing it with known reference samples; a results grid can be turned into an identification key.
goals: I can test five known powders and the scene powder systematically and record the results in a grid.
I can use my results to identify the scene powder and turn the grid into a flowchart key.

flow.what: Three chromatography recap questions; dry Week 3 chromatograms handed back and stuck into the Week 3 worksheet box; Today slide with the two goals and key words (about 1 minute). Slides 2 to 3.
Teacher holds up the Evidence 3 bag: 'White. So are five things in the canteen cupboard. Which one?' Hands-up vote (opinion, to be tested); numbers on the board. Slide 4.

Three tests and what a positive result looks like (water: dissolves?; vinegar: fizzes?; iodine: blue-black?; plus the magnifier); model one powder; be systematic (same amount, same order, clean spoon for each powder); safety slide, goggles on, Safety Officer checks. Students copy 'what to look for' into the grid header. Slides 5 to 7.

Groups test the five known powders and the scene powder (magnifier, water, 5 drops of vinegar, 1 drop of iodine), scene powder last, Recorder fills the grid (12 minutes); the teacher circulates and controls the iodine bottle (or gives it to Safety Officers); at minute 12 the teacher calls 'tests finished, start your key'; flowchart key (6 minutes). Slides 8 to 10.

Identify the powder with the frame (baking soda: it fizzes and does not turn blue-black); linked suspects Chef Zhou and Dr Huang, ruled out Lily and Max; evidence log row 4 and suspect tracker; confidence vote, without confirming any suspect; exit ticket; logbook line if time. Slides 11 to 12.

one_pager.practical: Groups of 4 test five known white powders and the scene powder with a magnifier, water, vinegar and (optional) iodine on a spotting tile, recording every result in a grid.
one_pager.assessment: Results grid and flowchart key on the worksheet; evidence log row 4, suspect tracker 'Powder' column and confidence row in the case file; exit ticket (names the powder, the test that proved it and the two linked suspects, plus the Today I can ticks) shows whether students can justify an identification with a test result; logbook line if time, otherwise evidence log row 4 counts.
hazards: Eye splashes from vinegar and iodine: goggles on before either is opened; if anything gets in an eye, rinse with plenty of water and tell the teacher.
Food allergy (wheat flour, corn): check the allergy list; anyone affected does not handle flour or cornflour and takes the Recorder role.
Never taste or eat any powder or liquid.
Iodine stains skin and clothes: optional, teacher or Safety Officer only, one drop with the dropper.
Powder dust: do not blow or shake powders.
Wash hands after the practical.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'The scene powder matches ___ because it ___.', 'When we added vinegar, it ___.', 'This evidence is strong / weak because ___.' Chinese welcome during testing and pair talk. Traps: 'soluble' vs 'solvent' (last week); 'fizz' is new; 'dissolve' is a verb, 'soluble' an adjective; 'starch' is unfamiliar. Band 1: sit beside a Band 3 language buddy (reads the Chinese line and explains, never writes the answer), start as Measurer, record with ticks, crosses or pictures using the picture key, use the sorting strip for Core c; My thinking and the exit ticket may be in Chinese. Run Say, show, check on Slide 8.
watch_out: Students rush the vinegar test and miss weak fizzing: tell them to watch the well for 10 seconds.
One spoon used for several powders contaminates the results: one clean spoon per powder (this sets up Week 9).
Many groups will name Dr Huang: keep a neutral face and do not confirm or deny; ask how sure they are.
one_pager.next_week_link: Week 5 (the mystery liquid plus checkpoint): print the checkpoint papers, print the pH colour chart in colour and laminate it, make the red cabbage indicator the day before (25 minutes, refrigerate) and allow 15 minutes on the day for the soap solution, baking soda solution and scene liquid. Keep the Week 4 worksheets in the case files (unfinished Stretch keys can be the Week 5 Do Now; the results grid returns in Weeks 7 and 8). Put the key poster up from Week 5. Keep unopened Evidence 3 bags, pots and black card for Powder 2 in Weeks 7 and 8.

one_pager.big_idea: An indicator changes colour to show whether a liquid is an acid, neutral or an alkali; comparing an unknown with reference samples on the same indicator places it on the pH scale, but an indicator cannot tell us exactly which substance it is.
goals: I can use red cabbage indicator and reference samples to decide whether the scene liquid is an acid, neutral or an alkali, and estimate its pH.
I can notice when a new piece of evidence does not fit the others, and suggest explanations that could be checked.

flow.what: Checkpoint papers on desks before students arrive; start the 10-minute timer once all are seated; read the English stem then the Chinese gloss line if asked; collect at exactly 10 minutes, then show the Today slide while counting papers. Slides 2 to 3.
Teacher demo: a little vinegar into a cup of purple indicator (pink), baking soda solution into another (blue-green); students call out the colours. Slide 4.
Acid, neutral, alkali and the pH scale with the colour chart; safety slide; goggles on; students copy the colour key into the results table header. Slides 5 to 7.

Say, show, check on Slide 8, then groups add 10 drops of each reference liquid and the scene liquid to the six ready-filled indicator cups on white paper, record colour, type and pH, match with the suspect cards and update the tracker. Teacher checks same drops in every cup; at minute 11 calls 'finish recording, compare with suspect cards'. Slides 8 to 9.

'Something does not fit' slide: pair talk in any language on why the liquid does not fit; one idea per sticky note for the Ideas Parking Board (no answer given); evidence log row 5 and confidence; exit ticket with goal self-check; introduce the incoming teacher. Slides 10 to 12.

one_pager.practical: Groups test five reference liquids and the scene liquid (Evidence 4) with ready-filled cups of red cabbage indicator, read the colour and pH against the colour chart, and match the scene liquid to the suspects.
one_pager.assessment: Checkpoint (10 minutes, 12 marks) marked with the mark scheme and entered in tracker column Q before the handover note (bands 0 to 3, 4 to 6, 7 to 9, 10 to 12). Results table (Core a); evidence log row 5 and the suspect tracker 'Liquid' column; exit ticket (alkali, pH about 9, Dr Huang 3 of 4) with goal self-check; Ideas Parking Board sticky notes photographed for the incoming teacher (Week 9). Logbook line if time, otherwise evidence log row 5 counts.
hazards: Eye splashes from indicator, vinegar, lemon juice and soap solution: goggles on before any liquid is opened; if liquid gets in an eye, rinse with plenty of water and tell the teacher.
Never taste or drink any liquid.
Hot water: only the teacher uses it, to make the indicator the day before; students never handle hot water or the kettle.
Spills and wet floor: wipe up spills straight away.
Lemon juice is a food material: check the allergy list.
Wash hands after the practical.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'The scene liquid turned ___ , so it is ___ with a pH of about ___ .' 'This sample matches ___ because ___ .' 'The liquid evidence does not fit ___ because ___ .' 'One problem with this evidence is ___ .' Chinese is welcome in pair talk, on sticky notes, in My thinking and on the exit ticket. On the checkpoint the teacher reads the English stem, then the Chinese gloss line; Chinese is accepted for every written answer. Traps: 'acid' (noun) and 'acidic' (adjective) are both fine; the spelling of 'alkali'; 'neutral' is not 'natural'. Band 1: sit beside the language buddy (explains in Chinese, never writes the answer); dropper job first; Core a) copied from the bilingual laminated chart (colour word, 酸性, 中性 or 碱性, pH number); Core b) from the Chinese frame and word bank; Core c) copy two row labels; Core d) from the suspect picture cue. Stretch and Challenge are glossed, not required.
watch_out: The scene liquid must turn blue-green, not purple: test it yourself before the lesson (add a pinch of baking soda if the soap solution only goes blue-purple) and use bottled or purified water for the indicator and the water reference.

Keep the checkpoint to exactly 10 minutes and never cut it. If time is short, test only lemon juice, water, soap solution and the scene liquid, drop Stretch c) and Challenge, and take sticky-note ideas orally.

Do not explain why the liquid does not fit or confirm any suspect (the mop water twist is Week 9); the incoming teacher should not react to theories either. Watch for 'the indicator tells you exactly what the liquid is'.

For Week 6: print the scene footprint at 100% and check it measures exactly 24 cm; tape measures or metre sticks.

open_questions: Scene liquid amount: the kit card says about 10 ml per group (60 ml), but Case Bible Section 12 says about 20 ml per group (120 ml), and the Case Bible says it wins over lesson files. Which should the requisition use?

Baking soda solution: no file gives a recipe (strength) or volume. It is needed for the reference cups (60 ml), half of the scene liquid (30 or 60 ml) and the Hook demo. The requisition assumes 2 teaspoons of baking soda in about 100 ml of water. Is that right?
Paper towels and table cloths: the kit card gives no numbers (the requisition assumes 3 towels per group, 18, and 6 cloths). Confirm, or use the lab's own supply.
Hook demo: how much vinegar and baking soda solution is 'a little'? The requisition adds 10 ml of vinegar. Should the teacher wear goggles for the demo? They are not listed.

Checkpoint paper: Checkpoint_Y8.md says one side of A4, but the designed paper is 2 A4 pages ('turn over'). Print double-sided on one sheet, as assumed here? No spares are stated; 25 per class assumed (24 plus the incoming teacher's copy).

Checkpoint timing: Checkpoint_Y8.md Section 0 says the checkpoint runs after the mystery liquid test, but the lesson plan and Teacher Guide Section 3 put it first, in place of the Do Now. The lesson plan order is used here; should Checkpoint_Y8.md be corrected?

The recipes imply kitchen tools and containers (knife, chopping board, grater, teaspoon, measuring jug, stirring spoon, and a jug or bottle each for the soap solution, baking soda solution and scene liquid), but no file lists them. Are they in the prep room or canteen?

Ideas Parking Board: one header and one wall space are stated. With several classes, does each class get its own section or board, or is the board photographed and cleared after each class? Week 6 points to the board and Week 9 needs each class's own notes.

Indicator for several classes: one 500 ml batch serves one class and keeps for 3 days. Should a fresh batch be made the day before each class's lesson, or a double batch when two classes fall within 3 days? The requisition note says the canteen is asked for 1 head of red cabbage: how many heads per week?

The kit card's 15 minutes on the day covers making two solutions and the scene liquid, filling and labelling 74 cups, testing, and putting out checkpoint papers. That is tight. Should cups be labelled the day before (added here as an optional task)?

Kit card: it is marked 'Teacher copy' with no print count, so 1 is assumed. Should each tray also carry a copy for the Safety Officer (the Teacher Guide says the Safety Officer checks the kit card at the start of every Do phase)?
A3 wall pH chart: should it be printed in colour and laminated? The file says only '1 enlarged A3 copy for the wall'.
Worksheets: no spares are stated (24 per class printed). Add spares for new or absent students? Who cuts off the exit ticket strip (scissors are not listed)?

one_pager.big_idea: When two measurements are linked (a correlation), a scatter graph and a line of best fit let us estimate one from the other, but because people vary, an honest estimate is a range, not a single number.
goals: I can measure foot length and height carefully, plot them on a scatter graph and draw a line of best fit.
I can use the graph to estimate the height of the person who left the scene footprint as a range, and say which suspects fit.

flow.what: Teacher introduces self as the new case leader; 3 recap questions on the Week 5 liquid answered from the evidence log (alkali, about pH 9; Lily Chen and Chef Zhou; Dr Huang, 3 of 4); point to the Ideas Parking Board; Today slide with goals and key words (1 minute). Slides 2 to 3.
True-size scene footprint held next to a metre stick: 'Can a footprint tell us how tall someone is?' Predict with the frame and vote short, medium or tall; votes on the board. Slide 4.

Scatter graph, correlation and line of best fit with 6 example points; read off a value and give a range; model measuring safely and kindly (heel to wall, nearest 0.5 cm; book flat on head, nearest 1 cm; numbers, not names). Slides 5 to 7.

Measure in pairs (4 min); Recorders read group data while the teacher types it into the projected table (3 min); 'plot now' at minute 7, scatter graph (8 min); 'line and estimate' at minute 15, line of best fit and read off at 24 cm (3 min). Slides 8 to 10. If short: sample data card for everyone (saves about 7 min), plot 12 points, drop Challenge.

'Which suspects fit your range?' (Lily 158 cm and Dr Huang 165 cm in; Chef Zhou 176 cm and Max 182 cm out); 'Always, sometimes, never' pair talk (best answer: sometimes); update evidence log row 6, tracker and W6 confidence; exit ticket with Week 7 option vote; logbook line if time. Do not confirm any suspect. Slides 11 to 13.

one_pager.practical: Pairs measure each other's foot length (shoes off, to 0.5 cm) and height (book flat on head at a wall height station, to 1 cm), then plot class or sample data on a scatter graph, draw a line of best fit and read off the height for the 24 cm scene footprint.
one_pager.assessment: Scatter graph and height estimate on the worksheet (rubric strand 4 evidence for the final case file); evidence log row 6, suspect tracker column 'Footprint' and confidence row W6; exit ticket: height range, suspects who fit, goal ticks and each student's Week 7 option choice (needed before Week 7).
hazards: Shoes off for measuring (socks on): shoes under the desk, not in walkways; shoes back on before anyone leaves their seat.
No standing on chairs or tables to read a metre stick or scale.
Metre sticks held upright and close to the wall, never swung; tape measures retracted slowly so they do not snap back.
Body measurement can feel personal: measuring is voluntary, numbers not names, no comments on size; anyone may use the sample data instead.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'As foot length increases, height ___.' 'The line of best fit shows a height of about ___ cm for a 24 cm foot.' 'The person was probably between ___ cm and ___ cm tall.' 'This evidence is strong / weak because ___.' Chinese welcome while measuring and in pair talk; Chinese answers count everywhere, including My thinking and the exit ticket. Traps: say 'height', not 'high'; 'estimate' is a noun and a verb; 'range' means 'from ... to ...'; a line of best fit need not pass through every point or through zero. Band 1: sit beside the language buddy; start with measuring (Core a) using the Slide 8 picture steps and the height station sign; run Say, show, check on Slide 8.
watch_out: Printers shrink pages: print the scene footprint at 100% ('actual size'), never 'fit to page', and check every copy measures 24 cm.
Measuring overruns: if fewer than 16 students are measured or it is slow, switch everyone to the sample data card at once; never mix sample and class data on one graph.
Students join the dots, start the line at zero or give one number: ask 'Are there about as many crosses above your line as below?' and insist on a range.
one_pager.next_week_link: Read the exit tickets before Week 7 and give each group one option (Soil, Paper, Ink 2 or Powder 2: group majority, then balance, every option at least one group, no more than two groups per option); this list sets the Week 8 kit. Footprints go into case files; evidence log row 6, tracker and W6 confidence row must be filled in. Groups stay at their usual tables for Weeks 7 to 10. During this week, for Week 7: soil from the flowerbed by the science block entrance in a jar labelled 'Evidence 6', a crumpled lab paper towel labelled 'Evidence 7', clear jars with lids, coffee filters, spare pens A to D, salt, vinegar and powders.

one_pager.big_idea: A good forensic test starts with a clear question, compares the scene sample with known reference samples tested in exactly the same way, changes only one thing, and is planned to be safe before anyone touches the kit.
goals: I can write a testable question for my group's forensic test and name what we change, what we observe or measure, and what we keep the same.
I can plan a safe method with reference samples, repeats, a risk table and a results table.

flow.what: Three recap questions on mini whiteboards or in the logbook (footprint graph, which suspects fit the footprint, why one clean spoon per powder); Today slide with the two goals and key words. Slides 2 to 3.

'New evidence from the forensic team': hold up the sealed Evidence 6 (soil) and Evidence 7 (paper towel) bags and the two lab questions; hand each group its option card; Reporters read their question aloud in English, then Chinese. Slides 4 to 5.

Six planning steps (question, reference samples, variables, method with repeats, risk table, results table); variables and reference samples modelled with the Week 4 powder test; one worked risk-table row (vinegar). Students copy 'We change ___ . We observe ___ . We keep ___ the same.' Slides 6 to 8.

Groups plan on the plan sheet using the option card. Checkpoint 1 at minute 6 (question and reference samples signed off); checkpoint 2 at minute 12 (variables, method and risk table signed off); then results table headings with units and the kit request. Early finishers: Stretch and Challenge. Slides 9 to 10.

'Would you rather test?': choose the fairer of two soil methods (slide Plan A or Plan B) and justify; 2-minute plan swap with the next group against the checklist; exit ticket; logbook line if time. Collect exit tickets, plan sheets and kit requests at the door. Slides 11 to 13. If short, skip the plan swap.

one_pager.practical: No practical: groups plan their own Week 8 forensic test (Soil, Paper, Ink 2 or Powder 2) and only look at sealed evidence bags.
one_pager.assessment: Plan sheet is the main rubric evidence for strands 1 (questioning and predicting) and 2 (planning), signed off at checkpoint 1 (minute 6) and checkpoint 2 (minute 12) and filed in the case file. Exit ticket: what we change, what we observe or measure, one control, one hazard and its control. Kit requests show what to prepare for Week 8. Evidence log row 7 (result left as 'Week 8').
hazards: No practical work today: evidence bags stay sealed and go back to the teacher.
Do not open, smell or taste any sample.
The teacher checks every group's risk table (checkpoint 2, then again when reading the plan sheets) before any Week 8 practical.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'Our question is: Which ___ matches ___ ?' 'We change ___ . We observe / measure ___ . We keep ___ the same.' 'We will repeat each test ___ times because ___ .' 'The hazard is ___ . To stay safe we will ___ .' 'I predict ___ because ___ .' Chinese welcome for group planning talk; the plan sheet is written with English key words. Traps: hazard is the thing, risk is the chance and size of harm; 'control' means a control variable and also a reference sample used as a control; 'method' is a list of steps, not the kit list. Band 1: sit beside the language buddy (reads and explains in Chinese, never writes the answer); start with Core b) (copy sample names from the bilingual 'Your samples' box, write 参照 or 现场), then copy the Chinese question; order the method pictures and write only the step letter plus amount and unit (for example 'T, 1汤匙'); copy the bilingual hazards. At checkpoints the Reporter or buddy may explain in Chinese; the exit ticket may be in Chinese with the English key words.
watch_out: Groups change two things at once, write a kit list instead of a method, or plan 'one go': insist on the 'We change / observe / keep' frame, numbered steps with amounts and times, repeats, and the scene sample tested exactly like the references.
Allocate options before the lesson from the Week 6 exit tickets (every option at least once, no more than two groups per option) and print the option cards to match.

Evidence 6 must come from the same flowerbed as reference A, and Evidence 7 from the lab's own roll (P1) with a pencil arrow along the roll before crumpling, or the Week 8 results will not match the Case Bible.
one_pager.next_week_link: Week 8 is lab day. Read every plan sheet, check the risk table and write one comment on each: plan sheets go back to groups in the Week 8 Do Now. Keep the option cards: they stay on the tables beside the plan sheets in Week 8. Build each group's tray from its kit request and the Week 8 kit cards. Keep the sealed evidence bags (the Evidence 7 sheet is smoothed flat for Week 8). Collect the reference soils A to D and papers P1 to P4 this week; pre-test pens A, B and N in salt water and vinegar (Case Bible Section 11); make K1, K2 and X the day before Week 8.

open_questions: Plan sheet: the lesson file says a two-sided worksheet, but the design is 4 A4 pages printed double-sided. Page 3 is on the back of page 4, so cutting off the exit ticket (first cut line, a little under halfway down page 4) removes Stretch c and all of Challenge, and cutting off the kit request removes Challenge b and c. Collect the plan sheet uncut, or print the second sheet single-sided (3 sheets per copy, 72 per class)?
The kit request box is meant to be one per group, filled in by the Safety Officer, but it is printed on every student's plan sheet. Should only the Safety Officer's copy be used?

Option cards: the spec is 10 per class (6 group copies plus 4 spares), and they are used again in Week 8. As laminated cards are not written on, should one reusable set of 3 per option (12) be made for every class instead?
Reference soils and papers 'now if possible, so groups can see them': no amount or container is stated for Week 7. Show the Week 8 samples early, or a small labelled sample of each?

The kit card gives about 30 minutes for all Week 7 teacher prep, including collecting the reference soils and papers if possible, but the Week 8 kit cards give about 45 minutes for that collection alone. Count the collection in Week 7 or Week 8?
Evidence 6 container: the lesson file and kit card say a sealed labelled bag; Case Bible Section 12 and the Teacher Guide prep calendar say a labelled jar. Which should be used?
Evidence 7: the same sheet is smoothed flat and cut into strips in Week 8. If one teacher has several classes, should one Evidence 7 sheet be staged per Paper group per class?
Kit card and Week 8 kit lists: no print count is stated (1 teacher copy assumed). Should groups also get the kit list for their option ('plan with these') when filling in the kit request?
No spare plan sheets are stated (24 copies, 1 per student). Add spares for new or absent students?

one_pager.big_idea: Carrying out a planned test carefully, repeating it and recording every result straight away (including surprises) is what makes a result trustworthy enough to present as evidence.
goals: I can carry out my group's plan safely, repeat the test and record results with units in a table.
I can say what our result matches, how reliable it is, and what it does (or does not) show about the case.

flow.what: Trays already on tables; plan sheets returned with comments; goggles checked for Soil, Ink 2 and Powder 2 groups. Safety Officer reads the kit card aloud (hazards in English and Chinese); group checks the tray against its kit request; roles confirmed. Today slide with the two goals shown while the kit cards are read. Slides 2 to 3.

'Next week the jury will ask you three questions': did you repeat it, did you test the references the same way, could it be contaminated? Lead Scientist circles the repeat number on the plan. Slide 4.

Safety slide for all four options, goggles on where needed; recording rules: record straight away, units in the headings, never rub out (one line through), circle anomalies and record surprises honestly. Recorder sets up the recording sheet. Slides 5 to 6.

Say, show, check on Slide 7, then each group splits into two pairs that run the same test in parallel (two repeats), scene sample last and tested exactly like the references, recording on the group recording sheet. Teacher runs the clock from the run sheet with checkpoints at Do minutes 6, 12, 18 and 21, circulates and photographs results at minutes 18 to 21; clean-up from minute 21. Slides 7 to 9.

Worksheet match and strength; Reporter round, 20 seconds per group, results written on the board under the four option headings; evidence log row 8 with other groups' results; exit ticket collected at the door; logbook line if time. Slides 10 to 12.

one_pager.practical: Groups carry out the test they planned in Week 7 (Soil settling bottles, Paper absorbency strips, Ink 2 chromatography in water, salt water and vinegar, or Powder 2 mixture tests) as two pairs running parallel repeats.
one_pager.assessment: Group recording sheet and individual worksheet are the main rubric evidence for strand 3 (doing and recording) and part of strand 4; both go into the case file. Evidence log row 8. Exit ticket: what the scene sample matched, whether the repeats agreed, and strong, supporting or weak with a reason. Photographs of every group's results for the Week 9 evidence board and Week 10 talks.
hazards: Goggles for anything with vinegar or iodine, and while shaking soil bottles; check every lid is tight before shaking.
Never taste any sample, powder or liquid, and do not drink the water.
Powder 2: allergy check (wheat flour, corn) before the lesson; an allergic student is the Recorder. Do not blow or shake powders.
Iodine stains skin and clothes: one drop, dropper only, Safety Officer only; returned to the teacher.
Soil can carry germs: cover cuts or wear gloves, do not touch face or mouth, wash hands with soap; soil never goes down the sink.
Plastic bottles only, not glass.
Scissors: cut away from fingers, pass handle first, count back in. Food colouring and felt-tip ink stain: one drop, caps on.
Wipe spills at once; vinegar in the eyes: rinse with plenty of water and tell the teacher.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'The scene sample matches ___ because ___ .' 'Our repeats were close / not close, so the result is ___ .' 'One result did not fit: ___ . We ___ .' 'This evidence is strong / supporting / weak because ___ .' 'One problem with this evidence is ___ .' Chinese welcome during practical work; results recorded with English key words. Traps: 'repeat' vs 'replace'; 'reliable' vs 'accurate' (reliable = repeats agree; do not push the difference now); 'settle' (Soil) is new; 'absorb' spelling. Band 1: the language buddy is in the same pair and explains in Chinese but never writes the answer; give a doing job first (timer or Measurer); the Week 7 option card stays on the table and the bilingual recording sheet lets the student be Recorder too. Worksheet order: Core b), c) (copy from the recording sheet footer), d) (Chinese frame, reason word; a Chinese reason counts), e) (tick the suspect grid or write 没有 or 全部), with a) copied from the plan sheet. Exit ticket may be in Chinese with a bilingual strength word from the word bank.
watch_out: Trays must be complete before students arrive: with only 24 Do minutes, a missing item costs a group its repeat. Check each tray against the group's kit request.

Students rub out odd results, change the method half way without recording it, or think a surprise means they did it wrong: insist on one line through, circled anomalies with a reason, and honest recording.

'A match proves who did it': Soil and Paper match things every suspect used, so they rule nobody out (weak); Ink 2 and Powder 2 only confirm earlier results (supporting). Never invent a result that points to one suspect.

one_pager.big_idea: No single clue proves who took the notebook; scientists rank each piece of evidence by how many suspects it fits, set aside evidence that is contaminated (with a checked reason, not because it is inconvenient), and judge the whole combination with an honest level of confidence.
goals: I can rank each piece of evidence as strong, supporting or weak, and explain why the puddle must be set aside as contaminated evidence.
I can write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning conclusion with a confidence level, and explain how tunnel vision could have misled us.

flow.what: Case files on tables: count each suspect's ticks in the suspect tracker (Weeks 2 to 6). Answers: Lily 3, Max 2, Chef Zhou 2, Dr Huang 4 of 5; nobody matches everything. Today slide for the last minute. Slides 2 to 3.
Week 5 Ideas Parking Board photo on screen; students find their own note. 'We parked these ideas. The jury meets next week. Today we check them.' Do not say which idea is right. Slide 4.

Strong points to one suspect, supporting matches two, weak matches three or four or something everyone used; rank the loop fingerprint with a hand signal (weak); a combination can be strong when no single clue is. Slides 5 to 6.

Minute 0: card packs and A3 boards; groups write matches and place cards (7 min). Minute 7: cleaning log card to each group; check scene map and sign-in sheet, set Evidence 4 aside, re-count (4 min). Each student writes a CER conclusion with a confidence level (7 min). Never confirm a suspect. Slides 7 to 10.

Tunnel vision cartoon (best answer C) and sort the parking board notes (3 min); expert witness roles and statement frames, each student starts one part (4 min); self-assessment slip (4 min); exit ticket (1 min). Slides 11 to 13.

one_pager.practical: No practical: groups build an A3 evidence board from printed evidence cards, then use the hidden cleaning log card to set aside the contaminated puddle and re-count.
one_pager.assessment: CER conclusion and evidence board (photographed) are the main rubric evidence for strands 4 and 5 and go into the case file. Evidence log row 9 and the CER count as the logbook entry. Self-assessment slips collected and compared with your judgement. Exit ticket: which clue was set aside, why, and which suspect matches all the reliable clues. Collect all case files and draft rubric levels for strands 1 to 5 before Week 10.
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Soil groups' settling bottles stay sealed on the windowsill: look only, do not open.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'This evidence is strong / supporting / weak because it matches ___ suspects.' 'Evidence 4 is contaminated because ___ .' 'We claim that ___ took the notebook. The evidence is ___ . This shows ___ because ___ .' 'We are ___ confident, but not certain, because ___ .' 'One problem with this evidence is ___ .' Chinese welcome for board building and the tunnel vision talk; written conclusions use English key words. Traps: contamination (noun) vs contaminated (adjective); evidence is uncountable ('three pieces of evidence'); 'bias' is about how we think, not unfairness to a person; confident vs confidence. Band 1: sit with the language buddy (reads and explains in Chinese, never writes the answer); count suspect names against the bilingual strength key; copy 拖把桶 and the clue and suspect names from the fold-under word bank (小心地滑 is on slide 8, not in the word bank); Chinese answers count for every Core task, including the exit ticket.
watch_out: Keep the cleaning log cards sealed in the envelope until minute 7 of the Do phase, after every group has a first board; then give a full minute of quiet.
Never confirm the culprit, even when every group says Dr Huang, and nobody reads a model conclusion aloud: the reveal is in Week 10.
Evidence is set aside only with a checked reason; high confidence is not certainty; contamination does not mean anyone did wrong.
one_pager.next_week_link: Collect every case file and self-assessment slip today and photograph every board; draft rubric levels for strands 1 to 5 before Week 10 (strand 6 is judged from the talk). one_pager.big_idea: Scientists communicate and defend their conclusions with evidence, answer hard questions honestly (including what their evidence does not show), and accept the result of checking, even if it proves them wrong.
goals: I can explain one piece of evidence to the Court of Science clearly: what we tested, how, what it shows and how sure we are.
I can answer or ask a question about evidence, and reach a verdict based on the strength of all the evidence.

flow.what: Final skills check, the same paper as Week 1, worked alone: papers face down on desks before students arrive, timer starts when all are seated, 5-minute warning, collected at once. The Today slide (Slide 3) is shown while papers are collected; the check is never shortened. Slides 2 to 3.

The teacher becomes the judge: 'The Court of Science is now in session.' A student reads the Chinese goals; the teacher shows the order of witnesses and who asks each question; experts put on badges; juries pick up question cards and jury notes. Slide 4.

Groups take the stand in evidence order (Fingerprint, Ink, Powder, Liquid, Footprint, Soil and paper): 90-second talk plus one jury question from the next group (about 30 seconds; the Fingerprint group asks Soil and paper). Everyone fills in jury notes and one peer feedback slip; the teacher records strand 6 on the talk record. Slides 5 to 7.

flow.phase: Think and Reflect: verdict and true ending
flow.what: Students write their own verdict and confidence on the exit ticket (30 seconds), then vote by show of hands; the teacher reads the reveal card aloud (optional frosty notebook prop), a confident Chinese reader reads the 概要 lines, 'Case closed'. Slide 11 only if the verdict was wrong or split. Slides 8 to 11.

flow.phase: Think and Reflect: survey and certificates
flow.what: Interest survey (3 minutes); thanks and certificates, or 'case closed' thanks if certificates come later (2 minutes). Slides 12 to 13.

one_pager.practical: No practical: groups give 90-second expert witness talks at the Court of Science and answer one jury question; the class acts as jury and votes on a verdict.
one_pager.assessment: Final skills check (same paper as Week 1, out of 20; tracker column S, 'W10 skills check'); interest survey (W10 S1 to S6); strand 6 Communicating from the talk record (judged on clarity of the science, not grammar or accent); final case file for strands 1 to 5, checked with the final case file checklist; verdict exit ticket and evidence log row 10; peer feedback slips into case files (not marked). Then award rules, Most Improved, certificates and skills reports.
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
Optional notebook prop from the freezer: cold and wet; pass it round in its bag, not out of it.
one_pager.language_note: Frames on the stand: 'We tested ___ . We compared it with ___ . The result was ___ . This matches ___ . This evidence is strong / supporting / weak because ___ .' Answering: 'That is a good question. Our evidence shows ___ , but it does not show ___ .' Asking: read the card aloud. Verdict: 'My verdict is ___ because ___ .' Students may glance at or read their frame; a student who freezes may give one sentence in Chinese and then the key words in English (say this tip before witness 1). Band 1: sits beside the language buddy (reads the Chinese lines, never writes the answer); reads their part from the Week 9 statement frame, which has the Chinese beneath each English frame; in the jury notes writes the strength word by counting the suspect names the expert states (one 有力, two 支持性, three or more 薄弱, or 搁置) and copies words and names from the fold-under word bank; writes the exit ticket reason in Chinese with 我的裁决是___，因为___。 After the English ending, a confident Chinese reader reads the four 概要 lines on the reveal card. Chinese answers count for every Core task.
watch_out: The skills check is never shortened and must run as in Week 1: same unaltered paper, same access arrangements, dictionaries closed and put away, 5-minute warning, collected at once. Do not go through answers or return papers until marking and tracker entry are done.

Talks overrun: 90 seconds plus one question each; if a talk passes 2 minutes in total, thank the group and move on. If time is short, cut talks to 75 seconds and ask only three jury questions (after talks 2, 4 and 6); never skip the verdict and the true ending.

Final certificates usually cannot be given today (awards need strand 6 and the marked skills check): thank the class and present them within a week, or give only awards already fixed from the Week 9 draft levels.

Keep the case files (with each group's peer feedback slips and a reveal card) for marking and storage; return Week 1 and Week 10 skills check papers only after all of this.
